description: Every row of passes/additions.json (steps A, C and V), read by a second reader (Claude Opus, tools/transcription/PRECISION_PROMPT.md): right, weak or wrong, and whether the label fits.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: 'Capable d'obligations et de droits' is Wolff's definition of the moral person as subject of obligations and rights, which Wolff's own JG preface also applies to nations.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Renders Wolff JG § 3: because a nation's nature differs from man's, applying natural law to it gives different results; Vattel reverses the order and adds his own words, so this is not close paraphrase.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same Wolffian definition of the necessary law of nations as natural law applied to nations (JG § 4 words it closer, but Inst. § 1088 states it too).

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's explanation that the law is called necessary because nations are absolutely bound by it compresses Wolff §6 on the necessary obligation of the necessary law of nations.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: That natural law applied to states is the law of nations is the Hobbes view reported in Pufendorf II.3.23, but the idea is common stock and Vattel's formula follows Wolff, so this passage shows no specific debt to Pufendorf.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Inst. § 1088 gives the same argument (men uniting in states cannot shed natural obligation, so nations owe the same duties as individuals) and the same sequence that follows in Vattel: necessary or natural law of nations, Grotius's internal law.

rows.label: citation
rows.reason: Vattel names Grotius for the 'droit des gens interne' that binds in conscience, which Grotius expresses as the rules binding in conscience as opposed to the external law of nations (III.20.53); the attribution itself is translated from Wolff, JG Prol. §4.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff's attribution to Grotius and his followers of the name 'jus gentium internum' is the same specific claim (JG Prolegomena § 4 is still closer, adding 'in conscientia' and 'naturale').

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same inference from the necessary, immutable obligation of the necessary law of nations to the rule that no nation can release itself or another from it.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel Prelim. 9 follows Wolff JG 6: no nation can release itself or another from the necessary law, and some licence must be tolerated between nations even though it stays illicit in conscience.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's 'considérées comme autant de personnes libres qui vivent ensemble dans l'état de nature' renders Wolff's specific formula 'spectantur tanquam personae liberae in statu naturali viventes'.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Near translation of JG § 2's formula 'Gentes spectantur tanquam personae singulares liberae in statu naturali viventes'.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff's INST § 1090 point that nations must perfect themselves and their state by joining forces, so nature set up a society among them, appears as the purpose of the society of nations.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff's specific point, that natural obligation is never itself imperfect and imperfection lies only in the lack of a right to compel, is Vattel's internal/external distinction.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: The pair of sovereignties given in fief and sovereigns making themselves feudatories matches feudum datum/oblatum, but that is a standard feudal-law distinction and Wolff's section is not about states.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel follows Grotius I.3.23's main argument; the note's franc fief reduced to honouring the lord only loosely matches 'simple reconnoissance honorifique', which is a generic idea.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Avoiding the troubles of repeated elections as the reason for making the crown hereditary is a commonplace; nothing ties Vattel to this passage of Barbeyrac's preface.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Regency by law or the nation in a minority is common doctrine; Grotius I.3.15 uses it to distinguish patrimonial kingdoms, and nothing in Vattel's short § 64 points to this passage rather than Wolff or the common stock.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Regency of an incapable king by law or by the people, acting in the king's name, is stock public law; Wolff §981 states it in passing in a passage on who may make peace.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both say that a regent appointed for a minority or for incapacity holds royal authority for the fixed time, but this is a stock point about regency. Vattel's stress on exercising it in the king's name is his own.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: That a regent holds the royal authority but exercises it in the king's name is the ordinary notion of regency. Vattel does not take up Pufendorf's polemic against Grotius over temporary monarchs.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: That a regent or tutor of an incapable king governs in the king's name is common doctrine; JG § 980 states it in passing in the chapter on peace-making, and nothing specific links Vattel's § 64 to it.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel repeats Barbeyrac's Grotius II.7.16 rule word for word ('né d'un mariage conforme aux loix du pays') with its aim of a certain succession.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Barbeyrac's note on regency defines a patrimonial kingdom in passing by alienation and control of the succession, but that is the stock definition and the note's point is elsewhere.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both say an unlegitimated conquest leaves the state of war in being, but Barbeyrac calls this generally admitted, Vattel's condition (just government, not consent) differs, and Vattel's note in this section points to Grotius I.3.12, not III.8.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff JG 214 justifies tolls by the costs of facilitating commerce, which no nation need bear 'gratis', with foreigners sharing the benefit; this is Vattel's argument down to 'rien ne l'oblige a en gratifier les etrangers'.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same sequence as Wolff INST §1036: the ruler must see that sufficient coin is struck and that its intrinsic value matches its extrinsic value.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same specific definition of good coin as coin whose intrinsic value answers to its extrinsic value, in Vattel's chapter on the prince's care of the coinage, as in Wolff's De cura circa monetam.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff Inst. § 1059 gives the same sequence: coin enough good money, give base coin an excessive value in calamities, then redeem it with good coin afterwards. Vattel follows it.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff Inst 1059 has the same sequence: coin given an excessive value in calamities must, once they cease, be exchanged for good coin.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: 'C'est un crime de nuire à sa patrie' is Seneca's commonplace maxim; Vattel's argument (love of country, ingratitude, perfidy) is not Seneca's (harming the citizen and man as part of the whole).

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: The 'engagemens' are the pledge of I.120 by which each citizen binds himself to all to promote the common good (JG § 135), and I.123 follows § 136; but the clause alludes to that obligation rather than paraphrasing it.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's paragraph follows § 136, but the traitor whose selfish heart lacks affection for others is a different claim from Wolff's remark that whoever hates his country seems to have put off human nature.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel I.123 follows Wolff JG 136 (De patria non nocendo), including its ingratitude point, and closes with Wolff's sentence that those who wrong their country justly earn everyone's indignation.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: 'Treating each according to his merits' is a stock definition of distributive justice; Barbeyrac's note on choosing the worthiest recipients is only a loose parallel.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Pufendorf only reports Aristotle's stock definition of distributive justice as distribution of honours among members of a state; nothing specific links Vattel's sentence to it.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Rewarding merit to encourage others and giving offices only to capable men is a stock precept on rulers; Vattel puts it under distributive justice, and nothing ties it to Pufendorf VII.9.9 on choosing ministers.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Honours as incentives to merit is a commonplace; Wolff's remark is about titles not being venal, and nothing specific links it to Vattel's sentence.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Giving offices to capable people is a stock point of distributive justice; Barbeyrac's specific point (do not prefer a needy candidate over a more capable one) is absent from Vattel.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: 'Offices only to those capable of discharging them well' is a stock maxim; Pufendorf's sentence sits in a passage on ranks, and the parallel wording is generic.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same commonplace sequence (attributive justice, imperfect right to rewards, regard for merit), also found in Grotius I.1.8 and Barbeyrac's notes; nothing ties the sentence to Pufendorf in particular.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same concession in nearly the same words: the sovereign/people may give offices to whom it pleases because no one has a perfect right to an office (Pufendorf III.1.3 after Cicero).

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: That no one has a full right to rewards or offices is the Grotian commonplace, found in several of Barbeyrac's notes and in Pufendorf; nothing points to this note.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Barbeyrac's note has the same case and analysis: a sovereign who passes over a worthy subject for a less capable one, or withholds a merited reward, does no strict wrong (there is no full right to office) but still sins against natural law.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both treat meritorious citizens passed over for unworthy men, with no perfect right to office, but this is common stock (Cicero, Grotius). Vattel draws a different conclusion (a just complaint of ingratitude), so the passage is not a paraphrase.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: The note shares the theme (no perfect right to offices) and the phrase about men without merit, but the wording is commonplace and Vattel calls the complaint just where Barbeyrac calls Catiline's a frivolous pretext.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: That affairs go well or badly according to the skill of those who run them is a commonplace; Pufendorf VII.9.9 (on choosing ministers) shares only this maxim with Vattel's passage on distributive justice.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Grounds the right to punish on Wolff's jus securitatis (INST § 89) and follows the chain to defence and punishment that corrects and deters (§§ 90-93).

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both derive punishment from the right to guard against injury: inflict an evil so the offender does not harm again and others are deterred by his example (Inst. §§ 91-93).

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's right to punish founded on the right of security, with ends of incapacitation, correction and example, follows Wolff Inst. §§89-93 (jus securitatis, poena emendatrix and exemplaris).

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's sequence follows Wolff Inst. §§1028-1030: security from injury is the state's end, so private war and punishment pass to the state, and the state, as a moral person, punishes public crimes.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff Inst § 1030 point for point: the commonwealth is a moral person that can be injured, so it may punish whoever violates public security, i.e. public crimes.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's definition of habitans as foreigners permitted to settle, set against citizens, renders Wolff's incola (peregrinus permitted to live in the country) of Inst. § 974.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Inst. § 1020 says the right of incolatus is transmissible; Vattel says the perpetual inhabitants' right passes to their children, giving another reason.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's banished man, expelled only from the banishing society's lands and free to live anywhere else, is Wolff's JG § 147 argument that the exile is not cast out of the whole world because the ruler has right only in his own lands.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's restriction of exile to a place to live in or a space to stay out of, left to the one who exiles, follows Wolff § 146 (locus a quo abesse / in quo commorari; regnat superioris arbitrium).

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's presumption that private property is granted with eminent domain reserved when a nation occupies a country is Wolff's ground in JG § 305 (dominium eminens reservatum).

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff § 305's 'dominium eminens tanquam pars potentialis imperii' together with 'imperium simul occupat' matches Vattel's eminent domain as part of the empire, conferred along with it.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's question and answer restate the first thesis of Wolff § 106: a river that separates two territories belongs to the nation that occupied it first.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's river section follows JG § 106 point by point, and his first rule gives the river's usefulness as the reason for presuming it occupied along with the land, as Wolff does.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Grotius II.3.18 already has the scheme Vattel uses: the whole river goes to the side that occupied first because the other came later, the middle applies in doubt, and treaties decide (Wolff JG § 106 is the closer relay).

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Pufendorf's rule concerns straits and gulfs; Vattel's first-occupant rule for rivers is stated directly in Wolff JG § 106 (and Grotius II.3.18), so this is only an analogue.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Barbeyrac's note gives a Roman example of a river held entire because boats were kept on it; Vattel's presumption from navigation or fishing is a general rule that the note only illustrates.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: The middle of a boundary river is a stock rule (also Grotius II.3.18); Vattel reaches it by a presumption that both nations arrived at once, not by Pufendorf's reasoning from arcifinious lands.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: That long possession must settle claims between nations or disputes and wars would never end is the stock rationale for prescription; nothing ties Vattel's brief rule specifically to Grotius II.4.1.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel applies the general doctrine of immemorial prescription to boundary rivers; Wolff §362 states the general doctrine, which is also common stock (Grotius II.4), and the content is not a paraphrase.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Treaty as decisive for a boundary river is generic; Vattel's rule sequence (first occupant, middle, treaties: 'Denique cum pacta sint servanda') follows Wolff, not Grotius II.3.18.

rows.label: translation
rows.reason: Renders Wolff § 106's closing rule on boundary rivers, 'quodsi res pactionibus definita, iis standum'.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff § 106 says treaties on river boundaries must be kept and that the difficulties push nations to settle them by pacts, almost all such law today being conventional; this is Vattel's advice and his remark on present practice.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel I.266 follows Wolff §106's river rules, and its close (conventions are the surest course, used by most powers today) renders Wolff's remark that today only conventional law applies.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Beyond the Roman rule (in Pufendorf IV.7.12), Vattel shares Wolff's naming of avulsion as the violent detachment of land by the water, which remains its owner's.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: That land which can still be identified does not change owner is a stock Roman-law rule (Wolff INST § 245 also has it), so Grotius's clause is plausible but not shown as the source.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel reproduces Grotius's moral reason against owning the sea: it suffices for all uses (fishing, navigation), so the reason for which property replaced the community of goods does not apply.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff JG §§ 120-121 gives the same chain: the use of the sea is navigation and fishing, which harms no one; the sea is a thing of inexhaustible use, which no one may appropriate.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel follows Grotius II.2.2-3: he gives the cause of property (the earth no longer sufficing without labour for multiplied mankind) and then denies that it applies to the inexhaustible sea.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Grotius II.2.3's moral reason, that the cause for leaving the community of goods does not apply to the sea, is Vattel's argument in nearly the same words ('n'a point de lieu' / 'ne peut avoir lieu').

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff § 128: coastal nations may occupy the sea as far as they can defend their dominion there, because the sea is a rampart and armed ships near the coast are a danger. Vattel gives the same limit and reason.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Near-translation of Wolff JG 128: it matters to coastal states that not everyone be free to come there with armed ships.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's statement that the parts of the sea so subjected belong to the nation's territory renders Wolff's conclusion in JG § 130 (partes maris occupatae ad territorium pertinent).

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's 'prétention vaine & ridicule de s'attribuer un droit que l'on ne seroit... en état de faire valoir' renders Wolff's 'Absonum est, si quis sibi arroget jus, quod tueri nequit' in the same sea-dominion argument.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel limits the occupation of bays and straits to those of small extent, which is Grotius's II.3.8 proviso and the one Wolff JG § 128 had rejected.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff's note to § 184 observes that nations often imitate others blindly and catch their vices, especially when biased toward a nation; Vattel condenses this.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel opens with Wolff's premise in § 202 (anyone may renounce his right) and draws the same conclusion, that a nation may restrict its trade in favour of another.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's sentence renders Wolff's proposition in JG § 207 (libertati commerciorum naturali minime adversatur) for treaties restricting trade with a given nation.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's 'punish or deliver to the offended state' is Grotius's aut punire aut dedere rule of II.21.4, which he follows with 'à la réquisition' as Grotius does.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's inference that full domain, a proper right to dispose at will, excludes all others' right is Wolff INST §195's definition and 'unde patet ... ceteros omnes excludere'.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel draws the same conclusion as JG § 293, from the same step: the nation's exclusive domain shuts out all foreign right, so no foreign nation can claim anything in its territory.

rows.label: translation
rows.reason: Vattel's marginal title renders Wolff's 'De limitibus territoriorum definiendis', and the paragraph gives the same reason (avoid encroachment and disputes).

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same argument and order as Wolff §284: since one may not extend one's bounds into another's territory, limits must be fixed clearly between neighbours to forestall disputes.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same specific precept and ground: territorial limits between neighbours must be fixed in order to remove whatever gives occasion to discord (Wolff JG § 286), in other words.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff INST § 1131 gives the same construction: the sovereign is understood to admit foreigners only on the tacit condition that they submit to the laws of the place.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Close rendering of JG §299: the territorial lord is understood to admit foreigners only on the tacit condition that they be subject to its laws.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: That foreigners must obey local laws is a commonplace; Pufendorf mentions it in passing on hunting laws, while Vattel's tacit-condition argument matches Wolff JG §§ 299-300.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff 1131 makes foreigners bound like citizens in the same circumstances, except where special laws on foreigners say otherwise; Vattel's restriction to general laws not tied to citizenship is a related limit but not the same point.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Pufendorf VII.2.20 grounds the rule that whoever enters a state's lands submits to its government on the security of the citizens, the reason Vattel gives for the same tacit condition.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Pufendorf III.6.2: by merely entering, the foreigner tacitly undertakes to obey the laws, since he must know this is required of all; Vattel has the same tacit submission on entry and the same reason.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff JG 300 (and 303) says that foreigners who enter a territory tacitly bind themselves to its laws; Vattel's clause renders this closely.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's tacit submission of the foreigner, who cannot presume admission on any other footing, is Wolff's presumption argument in JG §§ 299-300.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff §299 grounds the foreigner's subjection to local laws in the sovereign's imperium and legislative power over all that is done in the territory, as Vattel's sentence does.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff's note to JG § 299 rebuts the objection that civil laws bind only members of the state, the same point Vattel makes in saying laws bind everyone in the territory.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same sequence as Pufendorf II.6.5: those in extreme need, refused by those who have more than enough even when they offer money, may take by force; Vattel applies it to nations.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff Inst 307: extreme necessity gives a right to compel those who have grain in plenty to sell it at a fair price; Vattel's clause follows it closely.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: The 'de reste' condition on taking necessaries is shared, but it is the common Grotian condition (II.2.8) and Vattel's sentence (fair price, then force, from one who can spare) follows Wolff INST §305, not this note.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff INST §305 has the whole sequence: one wholly lacking necessaries may compel those who abound to sell at a fair price or take by force from one who can spare, by a residue of primitive community.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's 'l'extrême nécessité fait renaître la communion primitive' is Grotius's doctrine in II.2.6 that in extreme necessity the old right of common use revives.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: 'L'extrême nécessité fait renaître la communion primitive, dont l'abolition ne doit priver personne du nécessaire' restates Grotius's specific argument that property was set up with a tacit exception for necessity, which brings back the primitive community.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's clause recalls his II.117, which renders Wolff Inst 304: introducing property could take from no one the necessary use of things ('nemini auferri usus rerum necessarius').

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Pufendorf II.6.5's case of a shipwrecked man in a foreign country whose people refuse him help is the case Vattel states as a right of private persons and illustrates with Bontekoe.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: After the revived primitive communion in extreme necessity, Wolff § 342 extends the right to individuals of different nations, as Vattel's 'le même droit appartient à des particuliers'.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: In the same order as Grotius II.2.13-14 (passage of goods must be granted, then a toll may be levied 'pour s'en dédommager' of the expenses it causes), Vattel compensates for passage costs with tolls.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: The margin shares only the topic and Wolff's term 'habitation perpétuelle', which Vattel uses as his own standing term (I.213, II.125); nothing in the heading ties it to §149 specifically.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's references for Probus and Valens (Vopiscus Prob. c. XVIII, Ammianus XXXI, Socrates IV.28) are Pufendorf's marginal references to III.3.10, in a shortened form.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's note on Probus and Valens repeats Pufendorf III.3.10's cluster of references (Vopiscus Prob. XVIII, Ammianus XXXI, Socrates IV.28) and its Caesar reply to the Tencteri, so the reference is copied.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel II.136 follows Pufendorf III.3.10 (humanity to expelled peoples limited by the state's own safety, with the same Probus/Valens and Caesar examples).

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: As in Pufendorf III.3.10, settling exiles depends on weighing the state's interest; large warlike multitudes are dangerous and receiving foreigners can enlarge a state (cf. Vattel's Probus/Valens and Brandenburg).

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Vattel's right to refuse settlement to fugitive peoples contradicts Grotius's flat rule, but he neither names nor takes up Grotius and follows Pufendorf's correction, so the disagreement is implicit rather than open.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Pufendorf III.3.10 also denies a duty to receive a large, dangerous multitude of foreigners and tells the state to weigh its interest and place them so it has nothing to fear, which is Vattel's refuse-or-take-precautions argument.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff's rule that a nation judges for itself the reasons for refusing exiles fits Vattel's right to refuse a dangerous settlement, but the same point, together with the Probus and Valens examples, is in Pufendorf III.3.10, so nothing ties the sentence to Wolff.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: The maxim is Caesar's reply as Pufendorf III.3.10 gives it, in the same refugee context; Vattel's note quotes the same Latin with the same reference. But the text recasts it as a general maxim in other words, which is loose paraphrase, not close.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Pufendorf's checklist (whether more inhabitants are useful, whether they can be placed without danger) touches Vattel's concerns, but Vattel's specific advice to disperse refugees in under-peopled provinces is not in it.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: In the same setting, the reception of exiled foreigners weighed against the state's interest, Vattel takes Pufendorf III.3.10's point that welcoming foreigners enlarges the state.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: The rule that silence with a manifest reason raises no presumption of abandonment is common stock; Grotius II.4.5 ('la conjecture tirée du silence n'a plus de lieu') is closer to Vattel than Inst. § 460.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Fear and incapacity as excuses that defeat presumed abandonment are also in Grotius II.4.5, and Vattel's frame follows Wolff JG §363 (rationes silentii allegat, praesumtio cessat); the sentence structure differs from Pufendorf's.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Pufendorf says the blameless owner's loss is outweighed by public utility under civil-law prescription; Vattel says the owner must not suffer, the opposite claim, so it is not a paraphrase and no engagement is shown.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff § 363 holds that prescription fails against one who gives reasons for his silence and that the presumption falls when the contrary is shown, which Vattel renders as the owner's right to prove his property.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff's point that between nations the weak must often keep silent before a stronger power, so that silence cannot ground prescription, is what Vattel's remark about princes who silenced their weak victims applies.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Grotius II.4.8 argues that mankind's interest requires possession of sovereignty to become secure and incontestable with time, a fortiori from private possession. Vattel repeats the argument with the same key terms.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same argument from consequences as Grotius's reply to Vasquez: without prescription between sovereigns, disputes over kingdoms never end and there is no peace.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel follows JG § 372 (a mandatary's rights are defined by his mandate; apply the natural-law rules of mandate) and then states Wolff's rule that what the mandatary promises within his manifest mandate binds the principal.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: The elliptic term 'procuration cum libera' matches Wolff's 'Mandatum cum libera', which appears in this corpus only in Wolff, within the same mandate doctrine (a manifest mandate binds the principal).

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same specific reasoning: an engagement to an unlawful act is wholly void through lack of power, since no one can bind himself to do what the law forbids ('par le défaut de pouvoir' vs 'tire toute sa force du pouvoir de celui qui promet').

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's 'restreintes' to the persons of the contracting parties renders Wolff's 'ad personas paciscentes restringatur', Wolff's own criterion for personal treaties.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel defines real alliances by the things treated rather than the persons, the Wolffian formula of Inst. § 401 (rei magis quam personae ratione), against the Grotius/Pufendorf definition by the body of the state.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Right after the personal/real division, Vattel repeats Wolff's § 412 remark that it matters greatly whether a treaty is personal or real, because their effects differ.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Follows Wolff JG § 464 point by point: subordinate powers act by express mandate or within their charge, as far as the nature of the business allows.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff § 464 distinguishes conventions made by the sovereign's order, which count as made by the sovereign himself, from those that lesser powers (magistrates, generals) make by virtue of their office, as Vattel does.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel renders JG §464 nearly clause by clause: power arising from the nature of the business, especially when the sovereign cannot be consulted, with the besieged-town capitulation example.

rows.label: translation
rows.reason: Vattel translates Wolff's closing remark in JG § 464 deferring conventions of subordinate powers to the law of war.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's case is Wolff's sponsio: a convention by an ambassador or general made without the sovereign's mandate and outside the bounds of his office, binding only on ratification.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel takes Wolff §470's pairing: silence alone cannot ratify a sponsio, yet the sovereign should declare dissent as soon as it reaches his knowledge.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's 'les auteurs ajoutent' reports Grotius II.14.7: the king may take away rights subjects acquired by contract when the public good requires it, by eminent domain, the ground Vattel retains.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff § 462 gives the same presumption (in doubt the guarantee lasts as long as the treaty, because whoever asks for it wants security), but argued from the petitioner's intention, not in Vattel's sentence form.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel follows Wolff §§462-463: guarantee presumed to last as long as the treaty, but it can be restricted to the life of the guarantor or the parties.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: The whole of II.239 follows Wolff JG §§ 461-463 (the guarantee is presumed to last as long as the treaty, may be restricted to persons), and the closing sentence restates § 462's inference that a guarantee is a treaty, so treaty doctrine (personal/real) applies to it.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel restates JG § 502 clause by clause: as soon as what the hostages were given for is performed, they are free and must be released.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same rule in nearly the same words: the hostage must pay the debts he contracted before he is released (Wolff JG § 504).

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same inference with the same verb: the sovereign may dispose of subjects' persons for the state, therefore may give them as hostages (Wolff §510; Grotius III.20.52 also has it).

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's ground for indemnifying the hostage (public burdens must be shared equally among citizens) is Wolff §536's argument that all must promote the public good, so the hostage should not bear the burden alone and unpaid.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel II.252 follows Wolff JG 510-514 in sequence: the sovereign may give subjects as hostages; the subject is bound to go and may be compelled (512); a vassal may not be, unless also a subject (514); subordinate powers may also give hostages.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel restates JG §510: sovereigns and also lesser powers within the bounds of their charge may give hostages.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same proposition as Wolff § 534: whoever breaks faith after giving hostages wrongs the hostages.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's concessive proof (right to give hostages, but no right to sacrifice their liberty by breaking faith, an injury to the hostages) is Wolff §534.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Within the §534-536 sequence Vattel follows, the duty to free abandoned hostages answers Wolff §535's duty to redeem them, before compensation to them or their relatives (§536).

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: JG 536: the state must compensate the hostage's sufferings to him or to his relatives, by rewards; Vattel follows it closely.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff § 532: when faith is broken, the hostage is held as a captive (in perpetuum carcerem). Vattel keeps this without the alternative of slavery, inside a sequence that follows §§ 532-539.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's generous prince who will not use his rights to the misfortune of an innocent renders § 539: obsides innocentes, merum infortunium, generosi animi.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff § 539's release on condition that the hostage stay with the receiving nation and keep his goods there becomes Vattel's option of the hostage turning into a useful subject, followed by release on agreed terms.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff §539 lets the receiver of hostages abandoned by perfidy release them on conditions he chooses or keep them, which are Vattel's options.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both ground interpretation in the speaker's inability to foresee all circumstances, but that is the stock equity commonplace, with nothing specific to Wolff.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Grotius II.16.6 has the same Boeotian-lands quibble, the same reading of 'terres des Béotiens' as their ancient limits including what was taken in war, and the same verdict that the quibble would make the agreement void.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's case of a general promise of aid that does not extend to a manifestly unjust war is Wolff §660's tacit clause 'si bellum fuerit justum'.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel cites Barbeyrac's notes on Grotius and grants the point reported there, that fixed definitions of favourable and odious are lacking and hard to apply, before keeping the distinction.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's criteria of the favourable (common utility in conventions, equality between the parties, safe to extend) render Wolff's 'in pactis ad communem utilitatem spectant & utrique parti aequaliter consulunt', which are taken in the widest sense.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: 'Charge seulement l'une des parties, ou la charge plus que l'autre' translates Wolff Inst 809 'partem alteram saltem onerant, aut plus onerant alteram'.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff Inst. § 809 gives the same argument: a penalty is a burden, so terms containing a penalty are taken strictly. Vattel concludes that penal clauses burden a party and are therefore odious.

rows.label: citation
rows.reason: The note reproduces Grotius's Appian reference for the Carthaginian 'autonomos' (II.16.15 n.3) in an example Vattel explicitly credits to Grotius.

rows.label: citation
rows.reason: Vattel names Grotius as reporting the Rome-Carthage example; it is Grotius II.16.15 on the promise to leave Carthage free and the Romans' quibble over 'Carthage'.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: Vattel names Grotius for the Carthage example and repeats Barbeyrac's gloss 'libre, ou en possession de se gouverner par ses propres loix' word for word.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel names Grotius for the Carthage example and restates the Roman quibble that the promised liberty meant the citizens and not the city, keeping 'et non pas la ville'.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same example and verdict: the Romans' 'chicane' over what 'Carthage' meant in the promise of freedom.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel follows Grotius's argument and order: the liberty, though limited by the nature of the case, at least excluded forcing the Carthaginians to move their city elsewhere.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: The chapter title translates Wolff's JG ch. V title ('De modo componendi controversias Gentium'); the parallel with Pufendorf V.13 and its placement after interpretation is only generic.

rows.label: translation
rows.reason: Vattel's chapter title translates the Wolffian heading 'De modo componendi controversias Gentium', which the Institutiones share with JG.

rows.label: translation
rows.reason: The chapter title renders Wolff's 'De modo componendi controversias Gentium' word for word.

rows.label: translation
rows.reason: Vattel's opening sentence renders Wolff's 'fides Gentis Genti olim semper suspecta fuit' word for word.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel II.335 follows Wolff § 574 step by step (nations' faith always suspect, the plea that peaceful means would bring harmful delay, each nation judging, arms lawful by voluntary law), and this sentence renders the danger plea.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: In the same argument as JG § 574 (suspect faith, natural liberty, voluntary law), Vattel renders Wolff's clause that by natural liberty each nation's judgment on trying peaceful means must stand.

rows.label: translation
rows.reason: Vattel's sentence renders JG 574 clause by clause (voluntary law, arms in a doubtful cause to force a transaction, peaceful means untried).

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: In the same paragraph sequence as JG § 574, Vattel takes up Wolff's point that what the voluntary law lets a nation do with impunity can still be blameworthy and cost it its reputation.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's definition of talion repeats Grotius's 'souffre autant de mal qu'il en a fait' and, as Grotius does, names it the law of Rhadamanthus.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: The shared element is a stock definition of talion as suffering as much harm as one has done, which Pufendorf VIII.3.27 gives more closely along with the Rhadamanthus name. Grotius II.20.32 uses 'précisément autant de mal' in another sense and does not mention Rhadamanthus.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's definition of talion ('souffrir... autant de mal qu'il en a fait') and its name 'droit de Rhadamante' follow Grotius I.2.5 almost word for word, so the naming clause is closer than a loose paraphrase.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: The condition that justice must first have been asked for in vain is the standard condition for reprisals (Grotius III.2.5 attributes it to the jurists); Vattel's wording does not tie it to Wolff §589 specifically.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same specific doctrine: in a doubtful cause, the side that rejects the peaceful means of settlement natural law prescribes may be compelled by force to accept them. Wolff applies it to war, Vattel to reprisals.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel restates Wolff JG 289's rule that, between states, the members' goods count as the body's goods ('respectu Gentium exterarum ... bona civium pro bonis civitatis').

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: 'Est affecté pour les dettes de ce corps', grounded on members' goods counting as the nation's goods, is the thesis and proof of JG § 495.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Barbeyrac's note on III.2.2 has the same specific point: a subject whose goods answer for the state's debts may claim indemnity for whatever exceeds his 'quotte part', the reasoning Vattel uses for reprisals.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same specific rule: the loss suffered by subjects through reprisals is to be made good by the state, out of public funds.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff JG § 601: the innocent citizen should not bear alone a loss suffered for the people; he is compensated from public funds and bears only his pro rata share. This is Vattel's 'dette de l'état ... quote-part'.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same argument as Wolff §§ 589-590: citizens' goods answer for the nation only by the law of nations, so only nations and their sovereigns may make reprisals.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's 'il n'appartient donc qu'aux souverains' renders Wolff's 'jus repressaliarum non competere nisi Gentibus ... Rectoribus', with the same ground that citizens' goods answer for the nation only between states.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Follows Wolff § 590's further reason why private persons may not make reprisals (a matter for the state) and the next step, that subjects must get the sovereign's permission.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff JG § 590: a private person may use reprisals only with the ruler's prior permission, which Vattel restates as the practice of subjects seeking it from their sovereign.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff § 591 argues that, as with citizens' goods, their persons may be seized as pledges when justice is denied, the parallel with which Vattel opens.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's definition (seizing citizens of a nation that refuses justice, as goods are seized) and the name with its gloss follow Wolff § 592 ('Androlepsia, sive Viricapio ... pignorationis loco').

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Private force restricted by public justice except where it cannot be had is Grotius I.3.2's rule, but Wolff JG § 609 and others state the same rule-plus-exception; nothing ties Vattel to Grotius in particular.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same steps as Wolff § 614: the right of war is a right of majesty, so it belongs to the sovereign power, and how far depends on each state's constitution.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same argument and structure as JG § 614: since the people may divide or limit the powers it transfers, who holds the right of war must be sought in each state's fundamental laws.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's reduction of offensive war to pursuing rights or security, with the cases of obtaining one's claim, punishing an injury and averting a threatened danger, follows Wolff §§619-620's ends of war.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel lists the objects of offensive war as Wolff JG 619 lists the three ends of war, in the same order (obtain what is due, punish for security, avert a threatened injury or imminent danger), with matching terms ('sûreté', 'détourner').

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel III.10 follows Wolff §§ 749-752 in order: all who can are bound to serve, those unfit are exempt (children, old men, women discussed), useful functions are exempt when there is no necessity, and the clergy have no natural exemption.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's argument (functions are divided so the state is best served, so in the absence of necessity those in useful functions are exempt from service) is Wolff's in JG § 749 and its note.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Grotius III.22.4.3 has the same case of a subordinate who in bad faith claims more power than he has and must repair the damage, in the same wartime setting.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's 's'attribue un pouvoir qu'elle n'a pas, & trompe ainsi' echoes the note's 's'attribuoit plus de pouvoir qu'il n'en a' and its condition that the other party be actually deceived, on liability for an agent who exceeds his powers.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Cicero's line in Grotius III.19.1 that everyone values keeping faith is a generic consensus appeal; Vattel's 'comme en conviennent tous ceux qui ont du sentiment' shares nothing more specific.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's concurrence of justificative reasons and prudential motives (justice vs prudence) renders Wolff's twofold inquiry and his 'illae ut juste agas, hae ut prudenter' in JG § 621.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's account of justificative reasons as showing the sovereign's right to take arms renders Wolff's definition of rationes justificae in JG § 621.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's definition of pretexts as reasons given as justificatory that only have the appearance follows JG §§ 624-625 on rationes quasi justificae that are 'tantummodo praetextus'.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's pretexts, reasons alleged as justificatory that only look like them, are Wolff's rationes quasi justificae (JG §§ 624-625), which Wolff also calls praetextus.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both treat true reasons put forward as a pretext, but Wolff's case is a just cause masking motives of advantage, while Vattel's is reasons too slight to warrant war; this is a related idea, not the same argument.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel restates Wolff JG § 888 closely: since no nation can judge another, war in a doubtful cause must be held lawful on both sides as to its effects.

rows.label: translation
rows.reason: Vattel translates Wolff §635: injustice of war cannot be imputed to one acting from invincible ignorance or error.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same objection (the nation's preservation as a ground for war on a growing neighbour) and same reply (a lawful end does not license unlawful means) as JG §640, in the same sequence.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same syllogism as JG § 640: war is just only for injury done or threatened, so growth of power alone gives no right to arms.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel follows Wolff § 640's argument that, without any injury received, mere power with no declared intention threatens no injury and does not justify war.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both treat a neighbour's growing power as a ground for war and require will as well as power; Vattel's power/will pair is Grotius II.22.5's 'non seulement le pouvoir, mais encore la volonté'.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's objection that forced equality needs injustice and cannot be kept by lawful means applies Wolff's § 649 thesis (and § 648's commerce and succession cases) that a lawful growth of power cannot be limited for equilibrium's sake. It is the same argument, not a paraphrase of this sentence.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Pufendorf says a neighbour's growth by innocent industry gives no right to attack him; Vattel's sentence says commerce and industry would undo any imposed equality of powers, which is a different point.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's objection uses Wolff § 648's point that lawful growth by succession and commerce cannot be blocked for the balance's sake; it uses that point rather than paraphrasing it.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff §642 makes the balance consist in the others uniting by alliances to oppose an equal power to the preponderant one, the confederation remedy Vattel adopts in the same chapter sequence.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Matches Wolff § 649: nations have a right to keep the balance only so far as no nation's right is violated; Vattel praises the balancing policy as just while it uses legitimate means (confederations, as in Wolff §§ 650-651).

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff § 706 says the declaration contains both the announcement of the resolve to make war and the cause, the same two elements Vattel requires.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff § 737 makes informing one's own subjects the purpose of publishing a war, as distinct from declaring it to the enemy; Vattel gives the same purpose after his section on the declaration.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's notice of the declaration to neutral powers to inform them of the 'raisons justificatives' follows JG § 740: justificatory reasons are set out in declarations 'in gratiam exterorum'.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: 'Tel ou tel peuple' renders 'hac vel ista Gente': the declaration is notified so that other powers know whom the belligerent is at war with (JG §§ 737-738).

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's terminological split between publication to others and denunciatio to the enemy is Wolff's 'Differt publicatio a denunciatione' in JG § 737.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel follows JG §740: war is now ('hodie') published by manifestos, which are commonly called declarations of war.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff § 740 says that since no one wants to seem to wage an unjust war, manifestos set out the justificatory reasons. Vattel says the same ('raisons justificatives ... le moins scrupuleux voudroit passer pour juste').

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's III.63-64 on the publication of war follows Wolff §§737-740, and 'publiée, imprimée & répandue dans tout l'état' echoes §739's publication by a printed text distributed to courts and subjects.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff § 740 says manifestos also prescribe to subjects what they must do or not do during the war. That is Vattel's 'ordres généraux que le souverain donne à ses sujets'.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's exception for incorporeal rights that a third party granted with regard to who holds them follows Pufendorf VIII.6.19 (rights given to a particular person only), and Vattel then turns to the Theban debt case of VIII.6.20, as Pufendorf does.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Pufendorf VIII.6.19 makes the transfer of incorporeal rights to the captor depend on whether the original grantor meant them only for certain holders, which is Vattel's exception for rights a third party granted.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Barbeyrac's note to III.8.4 (the section Vattel cites) is where the debtor's neutrality comes in, binding him to pay the victor. Vattel's rights over sums 'que des nations neutres pourroient devoir à notre ennemi' take this up.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Barbeyrac's note concerns debts acquired with an enslaved captive and valid as regards neutrals; Vattel's point (debts owed to the enemy by neutrals are enemy property) follows Wolff JG §729 and Grotius III.8.4, which he cites.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same specific rule as Inst. § 1184 (incorporeal things are hostile, so debts owed to the enemy by a non-enemy count as enemy goods), but Vattel recasts the sentence rather than keeping Wolff's structure.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff § 729's rule that debts owed to my enemy by a non-enemy are hostile things is Vattel's point about sums owed by neutrals, but Vattel recasts the sentence ('la guerre nous donne ... les mêmes droits').

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff Inst. § 1198 gives the same two options in the same terms: confiscate subjects' debts to the enemy when payment falls due, or forbid paying them during the war.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel restates JG § 840: since the sovereign may confiscate enemy goods, he may forbid his subjects to pay their enemy creditors during the war, or take the payment himself when the term falls due.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Vattel restates Wolff § 840's right to confiscate or forbid payment of enemy debts, then corrects its 'durum ... malum necessarium' by noting European usage has relaxed 'cette rigueur'.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's two tests for a war alliance (justice of the cause, then the good of the state even when the cause is just, since the sovereign may act only for the state's end) are the two halves of Wolff § 658.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both allow war on the territory of the enemy's associate, but Vattel's sentence argues from absurdity and 'all forces' while Wolff argues that whatever is lawful against the enemy is lawful against his associate; only the general consequence is shared.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's general alliance 'faite avant qu'il fût question de la guerre présente' and his point that an auxiliary cannot claim not to be an enemy turn Wolff § 736 and its note (implicat esse medium et opem ferre) into rhetoric.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff §§733-735 holds that one who joins my enemy acts as an enemy, has no complaint if his lands are attacked and must blame himself for the danger, the argument of Vattel's rhetorical question; the sentences make the same point but do not paraphrase each other.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's 'exacte impartialité' and the grievance that favouring one side creates follow Wolff §§683-684 (no more favour to one party, lest it complain of neutrality not exactly kept).

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff §684 obliges neutrals to admit subjects of both belligerents to their territory to stay on business and buy what they need, as Vattel does.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff § 684: neutrals must let soldiers and subjects of both sides enter 'justi negotii causa' and buy 'res, quibus indigent'. Vattel's clause renders this phrase for phrase.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Grotius II.2.13 grants passage for just causes including a just war, but Vattel's 'innocent passage owed to nations at peace' follows Wolff's transitus innoxius; the shared doctrine is common stock.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same duty of innocent passage extended to troops as Inst. § 1182, followed by the same point that the grantor judges innocence; but the sentence structure differs.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same duty as JG § 686 (a nation must allow foreign troops innocent passage), but the sentence is restructured and adds nations at peace and private persons.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Barbeyrac denies in general that passage is always innocent; Vattel's remark that an army's passage is rarely wholly innocent is a common reservation and is not specific to this note.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Barbeyrac's note holds that letting an army pass is no office of innocent utility and that armies do damage (history gives examples); Vattel says an army's passage is hardly ever wholly innocent and gives examples of the damage.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel takes Pufendorf III.3.5's doubt, against Grotius, that troops ever pass without harm (few generals earn Pompey's praise), and he follows Pufendorf's anti-Grotian line again in III.123.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Grotius's note gives the Venetians' and the Pope's 16th-century excuse for granting passage (it could not be stopped without arms), the point of Vattel III.127. This sentence is about the damage Venice and the Papal lands suffered in recent wars.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: That passage turns a neutral country into the theatre of war is one of Pufendorf III.3.5's reasons, but Wolff JG § 695 gives it too ('sedes belli') and Vattel's Venice/Pope example is his own.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's Venice/papal-lands example illustrates Inst. § 1182's criterion that passage is not innocent if it fixes the seat of war in a peaceful land, in the same sequence; an example, not a paraphrase.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff §§ 695-696 argue that an army's passage is not innocent because it can make a peaceful land the theatre of war with great damage, and Vattel illustrates the same point with Venice and the Papal States.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel takes Grotius II.2.10's specific case and conditions in order: seizing a neutral place out of necessity to forestall the enemy, holding it only as a guard, and returning it once the danger is past.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel applies the rule of Wolff's neutrality note (what is granted to one belligerent must be granted to the other) to passage, which Wolff's next sections also cover ('utrique praestanda ... utrique deneganda').

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff §§684-685 requires the neutral to grant or deny passage alike to both belligerents and to avoid favouring one ('neutralitate non exacte servata'), as Vattel does.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel III.129 follows Wolff §§695-696: fear of the neutral land becoming the theatre of war justifies refusal, and a forced passage entitles the neutral to resist and side with the other party.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Grotius II.2.13.8 allows refusing passage to one marching to an unjust war, the same rule Vattel states.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff JG 804 holds the same thesis, but Grotius III.11.16.5 holds it too, and Vattel draws his examples (Milesians, Phyton) and citations from Grotius. Nothing in Vattel's wording points to Wolff in particular.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's appeal to today's practice of humane generals (honourable terms if the place yields in time, harsher if it holds out obstinately) matches Wolff's note to JG § 807 on what 'hodie Gentes moratiores' observe in sieges.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff §807 has the same sequence: obstinate resistance in a siege allows forcing surrender without conditions, but the enemy in one's power may not be killed.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel takes Grotius's (Polybius's) test and list: spare buildings whose destruction neither weakens the enemy nor benefits the destroyer (temples, public buildings, works of art). He also cites the Belisarius letter in the same paragraph.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff § 783 leaves the judgement of what the war requires to each belligerent, since nations are free and neither a neutral nor the enemy can judge, which is Vattel's argument for tolerating excess.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same argument as Wolff § 783: there is no common judge, each belligerent judges what is necessary, and disputes over abuse of force between belligerents would never end.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: The phrase 'tout lien d'humanité' and the idea that hostility does not dissolve all duties are shared, but Barbeyrac's note is on the use of traitors and the thought is commonplace.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff § 799 states that promises made to an enemy as an enemy must be kept and proves it, as Vattel does next, by a tacit waiver and the absurdity of treating to no effect.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel follows Wolff's note to § 799 step by step: treating with the enemy tacitly waives the war-right against the convention, otherwise nothing would be done, and it is absurd to suppose enemies treat to do nothing.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Grotius III.19.13 (keep faith even with the faithless) opens the sequence Vattel follows: tacit condition of reciprocity (§14) and retention by way of compensation (§15).

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: For a breach in a separate engagement Vattel allows withholding what was promised until the breach is repaired, a softened form of Grotius III.19.15-16 compensation across different contracts, after the same tacit-condition rule (§14).

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff permits falsiloquium only outside promising speech, since one must tell even the enemy the truth when promising; Vattel makes the same exception for conventions and treaties.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel reapplies to truthfulness the § 799 argument he already used in III.175: treating with an enemy carries a tacit engagement, otherwise it would be absurd and nothing would be done.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's reductio that deceiving under colour of a treaty would be mockery restates Wolff §800's point that promises to an enemy would become mere illusions, within the same faith-with-enemies argument.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's restitution by those holding goods taken in an unjust war is Grotius III.10.6, and he names Grotius III.10 in the next sentence.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Grotius II.26.4 and note 1 give the doubtful-command case with the rule that one who obeys acts involuntarily and is not to blame, the commander being the author of the damage. Vattel's 'non par leur volonté propre' and his 'le souverain seul est coupable' rest on that rule.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Pufendorf VIII.1.6's subject executing an order as a 'simple instrument' of the sovereign, who bears the fault, is Vattel's soldiers as 'instrumens dans la main du souverain'.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both name Grotius and narrow his view to the manifestly unjust war, with deference to the sovereign in doubtful cases (Pufendorf's correction, which Vattel goes on to argue). Vattel applies it to reparation, Pufendorf to military service, so the shared element is the argument, not a paraphrase.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Against the same Grotius passage (II.26.4) that Vattel names, Barbeyrac's note 12 holds that in doubtful cases the subject should obey, which is Vattel's position.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Pufendorf VIII.1.8 corrects Grotius in the same way: in a doubtful war the subject should obey and leave the account to the sovereign, who is presumed to know better. Vattel's duty to defer to the sovereign follows this.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's 'où en feroit-on, si à chaque démarche du souverain les sujets pouvoient peser la justice de ses raisons' recasts Pufendorf VIII.1.5's 'si toutes les fois que le Souverain donne quelque ordre, chacun pouvoit en demander la raison'. Pufendorf also says subjects must ignore some things, as Vattel says not all reasons can be published.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel takes the objection Grotius II.26.4 reports: if subjects could refuse to serve whenever they doubted the war's justice, the state would be ruined, since the sovereign cannot reveal his reasons. Wording and sentence form differ, so the label should be loose, not close, paraphrase.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Pufendorf VIII.1.6 argues that in doubt subjects should obey, since the sovereign is presumed to order only what is just and may have views they may not examine. Vattel pairs the sovereign's undisclosed reasons with the subjects' duty to presume them just in the same way.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Barbeyrac's note 19 gives Vattel's rule and its setting: reasons that cannot be published, presumption for the superior in doubt, dispensation only on full persuasion; but the wording is recast, not closely paraphrased.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Vattel explicitly rejects Grotius on soldiers' liability and adopts for those serving in good faith the exception Grotius III.10.5 refuses.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Barbeyrac's note puts reparation on the powers that began the unjust war and relieves the soldiers, which Vattel sharpens to 'the sovereign alone is bound to repair', amid Grotius III.10 material (vuider ses mains, restitution of what is held).

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's guilty sovereign / innocent soldiers by obedience is Augustine's dictum in Grotius II.26.4, within the same discussion of subjects serving in a doubtful war (incl. the objection that the prince cannot publish his reasons).

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's subjects who in doubt presume the sovereign's orders just and lend their arms as his instruments, leaving him alone culpable, follows Pufendorf VIII.1.6's argument (presumption, simple instrument, sovereign as sole author on whom the fault falls).

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Grotius II.26.4 reports the view that in doubt subjects should obey, that the one who commanded is the author of the damage, and that necessary obedience excuses; Vattel adopts this to make the sovereign alone liable for reparation, against Grotius III.10, whom he names.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Only the common idiom 'vuider ses mains' and the general duty of restitution are shared; Grotius's passage is about the Ninevites' repentance, not Vattel's point that soldiers are innocent but must give up what they took.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Grotius reports the commonplace (Seneca, Tacitus) that a subordinate carries out commands and does not judge them; Vattel's argument that government would become impossible is not there.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Pufendorf's argument reported in Barbeyrac's note (soldiers, ushers, executioners judging the justice of orders would make government impossible) is Vattel's sentence, but in different wording and structure.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Pufendorf VIII.1.6-7 gives the same argument: refusing on doubt endangers the state, sovereign orders are presumed just especially by public ministers, and the fault falls on the sovereign.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's grounds for acquiring captured things (expletio juris, the equivalent of the debt and the war expenses, and in place of the penalty) are those of Wolff § 859.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's 'rétablir dans leur premier état: c'est comme s'ils n'eussent point été pris' closely renders Wolff §895's restoration in pristinum statum 'ac si in potestate hostis nunquam fuissent'.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: JG 894 gives the same postliminium grounds: things and persons taken by unjust force are restored when they return, with separate just-war and unjust-war branches and the voluntary-law rule, as in Vattel III.205.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel states the truce case with Wolff's illness example (morbo) and force majeure, and gives Wolff's reason that the person knew the risk. The rest of his wording is closer to Grotius III.21.9.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same case as Grotius III.21.9: people held on enemy land when the truce ends may strictly be taken, but humanity and generosity call for letting them go; Vattel turns the release into a delay to leave.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Grotius III.6.27 confines acquisition of things taken to public wars in form and denies it in civil wars, which is the rule Vattel applies to subjects who take up arms without disowning their sovereign.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Barbeyrac's note has Vattel's specific argument: in civil war there is no common judge, a succession dispute or a rising dissolves the government into two bodies, and the war is treated like a public war between distinct states.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same two cases in the same order (people split into two parties, two pretenders to the crown) and the same conclusion that one nation becomes two bodies, as in Grotius II.18.2.4.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Barbeyrac's note gives the same argument: civil war with no common judge splits the nation (disputed succession or divided republic) into two distinct, independent bodies to be treated like two states at war.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: In Wolff §1007, a king in extreme necessity need not seek express consent to cede territory for peace, and the people's not objecting ratifies the cession; Vattel's 'censées approuvées & ratifiées par le seul silence de la nation' gives the same rule.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel IV.11 follows JG § 1007, and 'c'est au roi seul de juger des sacrifices ... pour acheter la paix' renders 'judicium de eo, sine quo pax impetrari nequit, ... penes Regem'.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff § 1007 holds that by transferring the right of making peace to the king, the people consented by that act to whatever peace requires; Vattel applies this to the French nation's tacit acceptance.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's closing caveat has the same structure and content as Wolff § 1007: the rules on alienating the state do not apply to parts given up or taken in war, where the people's consent is not required.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's two sentences follow Wolff § 1008 in order: private goods by eminent domain, and even persons by the sovereign's power.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's paragraph follows JG § 1008 (disposal of goods and persons by eminent domain and eminent power) and ends where Wolff ends, on what the state owes those affected, with a cross-reference; but Wolff only defers the question, while Vattel states the duty to indemnify.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Note (a) cites Wolff JG § 982 for the patrimonial/usufructuary distinction on a captive king's power to make peace, which Vattel rejects.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's opening renders the proposition of Wolff § 987 that the peace treaty ends the war and leaves neither belligerent any right to hostilities.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel IV.20 follows JG § 990 (amnesty as the first article, implied even when unstated) and gives Wolff's reason, that peace must extinguish every remaining cause of discord.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: The three points (amnesty as first article, usual today, implied even if the treaty is silent) follow JG 990 in order and nearly word for word.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff § 992 reasons that since neither party is condemned, what was taken in the war counts as lawfully held and matters left out remain as they are; Vattel follows this, amnesty included.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff § 992 derives that unmentioned things stay where they are and adds that consent to amnesty implies the same; Vattel follows the same sequence.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Same argument and order as Wolff § 998: soldiers acting within their duty before they learn of the peace are not punished, but what was taken after it was concluded must be returned.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: 'Restituer ce qui a ete pris depuis qu'elle est conclue', with the ground that no right remains, echoes Barbeyrac's Grotius III.20.20 closely.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Grotius's example of a tacit exception, promised auxiliary troops that need not be sent while needed 'pour sa propre défense', in the same sentence structure.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: For peace treaties, Vattel construes against the party who dictated the terms because he could have expressed himself more clearly, the same rule and reason as Grotius III.20.26 in nearly the same words.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff § 914's remark that kings may make truces for their lifetime is the specific idea Vattel turns into a proof that peace is real (a lifetime-only pact would be a truce); same idea, not the same statement.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Both ground observance of peace on the earlier-established faith of treaties, but 'obligation indispensable' and the back-reference are Vattel's habitual phrasing (cf. II.218); the structure is not the same.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's clause only recalls his previous paragraph's point that peace treaties bind whole nations, used here to urge fidelity, which Wolff § 1017 does not do; the bare claim is common doctrine.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel restates Grotius III.19.14, quoted in the preceding section, that all articles are bound to one another 'en forme de condition'.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel argues, as Grotius II.18.2 does, that an unequal ally remains independent and so keeps the right of embassy.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Grotius speaks of states partly subject to their ally keeping the right for matters in which they are independent (Vattel's IV.59 point); Vattel's vassals and tributaries 'qui ne sont point sujets' rest on his own I.7-8.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel grounds the duty to admit envoys, save for very particular reasons, on the nations' need to negotiate, as Wolff passes from the necessity of public business (§1044) to the duty to admit legates (§1045).

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's rule that a sovereign may not refuse a friendly power's minister without very particular reasons restates Grotius's maxim that envoys may not be refused 'sans sujet'.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Grotius's examples of the Romans directing envoys to their general and not to Rome are only loosely like Vattel's rule that envoys may be heard at a place on the frontier. There is no shared wording or specific signal, and an example generalized into a rule is not a paraphrase.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff § 1045 holds that envoys must be admitted unless the nation's duties to itself conflict. Vattel's freedom to refuse, 'fondée sur le soin que chaque nation doit à sa propre sûreté', with the maxim that one must admit, has the same structure.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Turns Barbeyrac's note (Grotius does not make refusing an armed enemy's envoys a general rule; only particular circumstances justify it) into Vattel's general maxim with the same exception.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Both justify refusing an enemy's envoy on a particular suspicion, but Vattel's example (an artful enemy dividing and lulling allies) is not Barbeyrac's Melesippus-as-spy and the type is common stock (Grotius's Totila, Buddeus's note in Pufendorf).

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel concedes Grotius II.18.5.1's point that only the power to which the envoy is sent is bound to his rights, but in a differently built sentence with different content words.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Vattel concedes Grotius's point that only the prince to whom the envoy is sent is bound ('A la vérité ...') but corrects his conclusion that third powers owe passing ambassadors nothing. His example, the Rincon and Fregose murders, is one Grotius's note lists as allowable.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: The Buddeus note concerns envoys crossing an enemy's land (Vattel's IV.85 case), whereas IV.84 says powers at peace must give passing ministers regard and safety.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Grotius II.18.5.3 says mistreating ambassadors in transit to another power is no breach of the law of nations (his n.4 even lists the Po murders); Vattel affirms it violates the right of embassy, using that case.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: That an insult to an envoy falls on his sender is a commonplace, and Wolff § 1064 concerns the host state, not the transit states Vattel is discussing.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Grotius's note to II.18.5 has the same 1541 Po murder, in the same context of ambassadors in transit, but Vattel's details and his cited source (Du Bellay) are elsewhere, and the case was a stock one (e.g. Wicquefort).

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff § 1065 makes envoys' security sacred because the common welfare of nations and the necessity of embassies require it, the ground Vattel restates when he calls the outrage the quarrel of all nations.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Wolff § 1064 grounds an envoy's security in that owed to any foreigner plus more for the sender's dignity, but Vattel's a fortiori concerns transit, which Wolff does not treat; the move is natural, and if it were borrowed it would be shared argument, not paraphrase.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Grotius II.18.5.2 allows a third power to kill envoys going to or from its enemies; in the same paragraph, after conceding II.18.5.1, Vattel says such a suspect minister may only be refused passage and never maltreated, which corrects Grotius.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Taking precautions instead of refusing passage when the reasons are not strong is Wolff's § 701 rule for armies, but Grotius II.2.13.5 already has it. Vattel transfers it to ministers, so nothing points to Wolff in particular.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's 'premier principe ... vérité de sentiment' that happiness is the end echoes Burlamaqui I.5.4's 'prémiére vérité dont nous sommes instruits par le sentiment intérieur' on the same point, and in the note it grounds obligation in the desire for happiness.
