rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's first principle (a 'vérité de sentiment' that happiness is the end of every being 'doué d'intelligence & de sentiment', and the ground of obligation) restates Burlamaqui I.5.4-5, including the phrase 'Etres doués de connoissance & de sentiment'.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Burlamaqui's motives-as-bonds account of obligation is close, but grounding obligation in the desire for happiness is already in Vattel's own Essai (1747), and 'lien' is the stock etymology.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's note defines the natural laws, as Burlamaqui I.i.1 does, as the rules man must follow to reach his end, happiness, and names them laws of nature.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Vattel grounds natural law in 'la nature des choses & celle de l'homme' and then adds God as author of all things, the Wolffian sequence of Inst. §§39-41.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: The 'etiamsi daremus' hypothesis is a commonplace, and Vattel's version (ignorance of God, the atheist still bound, God's will adding force) follows Wolff rather than Grotius specifically.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Repeats Burlamaqui II.2.3: God's end is his creatures' happiness as far as their nature allows, so he wills the rules that lead to it; the key clause is reworded.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Both make natural law oblige by the nature of things and by God's will together, but this concurrence is common to Wolff, Barbeyrac and Burlamaqui, and nothing specific ties Vattel's note to this sentence.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Vattel's 'same law, same obligation' from God's will and nature matches Wolff's conclusion, but he gets there through divine goodness and happiness, not Wolff's God-as-author-of-essences argument, and the coincidence thesis is shared stock (cf. Burlamaqui's concours of obligations).

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: 'Treated as an enemy of mankind' is a stock formula, and Barbeyrac uses it of a people losing esteem among nations, not of anyone who rejects natural law; no specific borrowing is shown.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: That man alone cannot reach his end and is therefore made for society is the common sociability argument; Vattel's note frames it as felicity, not Wolff's self-perfection, and nothing ties it to Inst. §44 in particular.

rows.label: close paraphrase
rows.reason: 'La nature elle-même a donc établi cette société' renders Wolff's formula 'ipsa natura societatem inter homines instituit' (JG § 7), which Vattel also uses in Prelim. § 11.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Both raise the stock question of the best form of government; Pufendorf only reports that most favour monarchy, while Vattel's limited-monarchy verdict and quotations are not from him.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Both use Theopompus for the lesson that limited power is more lasting, but Vattel tells the classical wife-and-king anecdote, while Barbeyrac quotes Sidney's 'least envied' version; this is a shared ancient example and nothing more.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Vattel's remark that the Spartan chiefs were 'très-improprement' called kings is Grotius's example (I.3.8) of kings dependent on the people who bear the title only 'dans un sens impropre', as at Lacedaemon after the Ephors.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Both treat Spartan kingship as sharply limited, a commonplace; Vattel's points (an improper title, kings put on trial and executed) are not in Wolff's definition of the regnum Laconicum.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Grotius I.4.8 gives the Spartan kings, dependent on the people, as rulers who could be punished with death (Pausanias), the point of Vattel's 'on les condamnoit à la mort'.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Vattel's gloss reverses Grotius's 'il ne s'ensuit point ... que les Peuples soient au dessus du Roi', but it comments on a quoted Latin author and states the stock popular-sovereignty thesis without taking up Grotius.

rows.label: open disagreement
rows.reason: Vattel's note draws 'nation above sovereign' from Mariana; it does not take up Pufendorf's rebuttal of the 'king for the people' argument, so only the topic is shared.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Vattel quotes Grotius's Annales on Brabant; the DJBP note only gives a bare reference to Meyer on Brabant for a reserved right of resistance, so the shared example does not show use of this note.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: The Brabant compact is a case of the clause in DJBP I.4.12 that frees subjects from obedience, but Vattel quotes it from Grotius's Annales (Liv. II), so nothing ties the note to this DJBP passage.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: The Brabant pact is quoted from Grotius's Annales; Pufendorf's general case of a clause freeing subjects from obedience shares the idea and the phrase 'affranchis de l'obéissance', which likely comes from the Annales translation.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: The note quotes Mariana. 'What common consent established, the same will can change' is a commonplace maxim that Wolff § 984 also states, with a proviso Vattel does not use.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Velly's episode illustrates the principle that infeudations or alienations made without the people's consent are void, but the note's wording and example come from Velly, and Vattel's surrounding text argues against Grotius, so there is no sign it draws on II.6.9.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Barbeyrac's note states the same principle, but Vattel's words are a quotation from Velly about King John, and nothing shows dependence on Barbeyrac.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Same maxim (no king may make his realm feudatory/tributary without consent), but the note quotes Velly on the French barons, and nothing ties it to Pufendorf VIII.5.10.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Vattel's remark rests on Boizard's evidence that the kings kept their debasements secret; with Pufendorf's Bosporan king, excused by necessity if later restored, it shares only the theme of debasement in necessity.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: The passage is Vattel's quotation of Boizard on the effects of debasement; it does not draw on Wolff's advice that rulers stop money-changers exporting good coin.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: The note quotes Boizard on princes who stopped debasing coin once the need passed; this is close in idea to Wolff's rule that bad coin be exchanged after a crisis, but it is a third author's text and nothing shows Wolff behind it.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: The words are Boizard's quotation of Philip the Fair's 1295 ordinance; they share with Pufendorf V.1.14 only the idea that a prince who debases coin should restore it later, which does not show any borrowing from Pufendorf.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Vattel's remark on bearing charitably with those of another worship and Salvian's 'God bears with those who err from piety' in Grotius II.20.50 share only the general tolerance theme, with no specific wording or argument.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Both deplore Jerome's (and Tertullian's) disparagement of marriage, but Vattel's Latin quotations are not in Barbeyrac and the complaint is stock Protestant anti-patristic polemic.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Barbeyrac's preface attacks the Fathers on marriage and says Jerome 'recommandoit le Célibat', but Vattel's Tertullian and Jerome quotations are not Barbeyrac's, and the charge is a commonplace.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: The note gives a Dutch example (taken from Grotius's history) of the rule Vattel takes from Wolff JG 82 in the main text. The note itself draws nothing from Wolff beyond an implied application of that rule.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: The note's point (Paykul left with the king's leave and sold his estates, so Sweden had no power over him) fits Pufendorf's rule on lawful emigrants, but the facts come from the cited history and the doctrine is common to Grotius II.5.24, Pufendorf and Wolff.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: The note repeats Grotius II.5.24's equitable limit: an individual may emigrate except when the interest of civil society (for example a war) requires him to stay. Vattel's main text adopts this along with Grotius's partnership analogy.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: The note's exception for a critical time is a back-reference to Vattel's own § 220; Pufendorf's clause (not leaving at war or on the eve of a siege) copies Grotius II.5.24, so nothing ties it to Pufendorf in particular.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Grotius II.15.5 makes Vattel's point that the ancients owed nothing to peoples bound to them by no treaty and illustrates it with the Roman rule on peoples without friendship, hospitality or alliance; that rule is the 'exemple des Romains' the note builds on.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Both allow armed help for foreign subjects persecuted for one's religion, but Vattel rests it on James I's self-defence argument, which he cites, not on Grotius's imperial examples. Only the conclusion is shared.

rows.label: verbatim
rows.reason: Only the standard German-law term 'jus detractus' is shared, which Wolff uses only as an example of retorsion; at most Vattel's definition loosely restates Wolff's example, so this is not verbatim and not clearly borrowed.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Both use Philip II's 1596 debt repudiation and its reversal on royal or state debts, but Vattel tells it from Grotius's Annales, with details Barbeyrac lacks, so nothing shows he took it from the note.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Vattel quotes Wolff's Jus naturae on standing by plain express words; INST § 798 gives a related plain-meaning rule (keep to common usage) but neither the quoted wording nor its certainty argument.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: De Witt's remark that general reprisals amount to open war fits Wolff's view that reprisals are war-like but not aimed at the whole people, but nothing ties the note to § 603.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: De Witt's quoted letter shares Wolff § 589's conditions for reprisals (only for one's own subjects, after justice is refused), but these are common doctrine and the text is de Witt's.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Both concern captives brought into a third power's port, but Grotius gives an ancient treaty exception to the rule that neutrals do not free captives, while Vattel's Dutch practice comes from elsewhere.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Vattel's note reports a Dutch and English customary ruling that prisoners brought into a neutral port must be freed, while Wolff § 834 forbids leading captives through neutral territory on a different ground; the shared argument is not there.

rows.label: shared argument

rows.reason: Both are Dutch examples of stopping neutral trade to blockaded ports, but Vattel's edict comes from Grotius's Histoire and is a different event from the Dunkirk case in the DJBP note.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Both discuss the same French rule that enemy goods confiscate friendly ones. But Vattel's note reports its annulment from Boreel's letter and shares nothing specific with Grotius's narrowing of it.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: The note gives the same maritime rule as Grotius III.6.6.2 (a friendly ship is not prize because of enemy goods aboard), but in a quotation from Boreel's letter; nothing in it draws on Grotius.

rows.reason: Grotius III.11.16 rejects obstinate resistance as a ground for refusing quarter, and Vattel's section, which cites that very paragraph for the Phyton story, calls the old maxim false.

rows.reason: Vattel cites Grotius for the farmer-sparing examples, and his note renders the Cyrus-Assyrian agreement in nearly Barbeyrac's words ('de part et d'autre', war only on those under arms).

rows.reason: Only DJBP III.21.1 and its note 1 have the term 'belli commercia' with its attribution to Virgil, applied to conventions that include the ransom of prisoners. Vattel repeats both, though he cites the Historiae.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: The only overlap is Anaxilaus's famine excuse, an ancient example. Vattel tells it at length from Xenophon to illustrate Spartan equity, while Grotius and Barbeyrac use it on surrender under famine.

rows.label: loose paraphrase
rows.reason: Same Xenophon example (Anaxilas acquitted), but Grotius uses it for a part of the state surrendering in necessity while Vattel uses it for equity in war, with a fuller account taken from Xenophon himself: a shared ancient example without the argument.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Grotius only remarks that histories are full of wars over mistreated ambassadors; Vattel's examples come from Marigny, so only the commonplace point is shared.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Pufendorf's limit of ambassadorial exemption to matters concerning their character and Vattel's view that a host may forbid ministers acts not needed for their functions share only the general functional view of immunity, with no specific shared wording.

rows.reason: Wolff's functional distinction between public and private acts of envoys underlies Vattel's remark only in general, and it is common doctrine with no shared wording or case.

rows.label: shared argument
rows.reason: Timur's secretary and Theodahad (in Grotius's note) make the same commonplace point that an envoy's sacred character depends on his good conduct, but Vattel quotes La Croix and nothing points to Grotius.
